extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, designers, and craftsmen concerned with ornament and detailing
extracted.subtask_short: designing architectural bases and wall decoration
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for proportion, form, and ornamentation of bases, spurs, wall veils, spandrils, tympana, gables, and shafts in medieval and Renaissance-derived architecture; focuses on when and how to apply ornament so as to preserve structural expression and visual unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of proportion and delicacy of curvature
rubrics_metrics.description: The various conditions of [a base] are beautiful or commonplace, in proportion to the variety of proportion among their lines and the delicacy of their curvatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty of a base depends on variety in proportions of its component lines and the subtlety of their curves. Evaluate profiles by how their proportions and curvatures express character; do not overemphasize microscopic precision of curvature at the expense of overall expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of curvature relative to general effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The precision of curvature is a matter of so small consequence in general effect that we need not here pursue the subject farther.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice broader compositional qualities to pursue extremely fine adjustments of curvature; small differences in profile curvature rarely change overall visual effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spur placement against rolls rather than on irregular profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: When Xb is divided into delicate mouldings, we cannot conveniently apply the spur to its irregular profile; we must be content to set it against the lower roll.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply spurs to stable, regular portions (e.g., lower roll) rather than to irregular or highly carved mouldings so the spur reads clearly and integrates structurally and visually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harsh straight spur lines; prefer noble curves
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a point of immediate necessity to substitute for its harsh right lines some curve of noble abstract character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the spur is often seen from above and is a focal feature, replace hard right-angled lines (c d, c e) with graceful abstract curves. Harsh straight edges on visible spur elements are an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gradated organic curves (e.g., salvia leaf line) for ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: It is simply its character of gradated curvature which fits [the salvia leaf line] for our use ... he may try how he can best substitute it for the awkward lines c d c e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When refining spur/profile details, consider borrowing gradated, organic curves (such as leaf lines) which scale well and create unity with the mass. Test substitutions (tracing, overlay) to ensure visual strength; avoid inserting delicate curves that make a spur look weak by being placed inside existing lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect proportional ratios between spur and roll
rubrics_metrics.description: In those shafts the quadrant a b ... is 2 feet 11 inches round, and the base of the spur d e is 10 inches; the line d e being therefore to a b as 10 to 25½. In Fig. LX it is as 10 to 24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow tested proportional relationships (examples given: spur base : roll ~10:24–25½) when designing spurs so the spur reads correctly relative to the roll. Use these proportions as representative measurements for Italian Gothic types; adjust logically for different shaft sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep outlines simple if preparing for richer decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Italian bases are merely prepared by their simple outlines for far richer decoration at the next step ... Northern disposition to break up bounding lines, and lose breadth in picturesqueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simple, robust outlines in primary shapes to allow for later applied decoration; avoid breaking bounding lines in ways that reduce perceived breadth (a Northern tendency noted as less desirable when richness is intended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rare/dubious plan forms (double spur, truncated spur)
rubrics_metrics.description: No. 2 ... is the only instance I ever saw of the double spur, as transitive between the square and octagon plinth; the truncated form, 1, is also rare and very ugly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with uncommon plan types like double spurs or truncated spurs—these are historically rare and often judged ugly unless carefully justified by context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine contours before ornament; decorate appropriately to context
rubrics_metrics.description: When the main contours of the base are once determined, its decoration is as easy as it is infinite ... I have merely given ... examples to which I shall need to refer, hereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix the primary massing and contours before adding ornament. Decoration is effectively endless but must be subordinate to and coherent with the base's principal form and its architectural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer vegetable/leaf forms for base ornament for unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater number of the best bases are formed of leaves ... The value of the vegetable form is especially here ... its capability of unity with the mass of the base, and of being suggested by few lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stylized plant/leaf motifs for base ornament because they suggest form with few lines and integrate well with mass. Entire animal forms under bases are generally riskier; only Northern Gothic architects consistently succeed with full animals in that position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve richly decorated rolls/ogee profiles for higher elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorated rolls and decorated ogee profiles ... ought always to be reserved for jambs, cornices, and archivolts: if you begin with them in the base, you have no power of refining your decorations as you ascend ... and you put your most delicate work on the jutting portions of the foundation, — the very portions which are most exposed to abrasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid putting the richest, most delicate moulding-work on the base; reserve such refined decoration for less-abrasion-prone, higher elements. Putting fineness low in the building is a 'barbarism' that weakens compositional hierarchy and durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base should express appropriate character (stern endurance or quiet simplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best expression of a base is that of stern endurance, — the look of being able to bear roughing; or, if the whole building is so delicate that no one can be expected to treat even its base with unkindness, then at least the expression of quiet, prefatory simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the expressive quality of the base according to the building's overall character: robust architecture requires bases of stern, enduring appearance; delicate buildings require simple, quiet bases. Do not repeat ornate 'beautiful' bases inappropriately along a colonnade or in sterner work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle spur ornament: boldness and simplicity for general service
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle spur may receive such decoration ... the ornament of the basic spur is best, in the long run, when it is boldest and simplest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ornamenting angle spurs, prefer bold, simple motifs that read at a distance and are durable; excessive delicacy weakens clarity and endurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Couchant animal bases are sculpture, not structural bases
rubrics_metrics.description: The fantastic bases formed by couchant animals ... are less to be considered as a true base than as a piece of sculpture ... deriving its value from its special positive fulfilment of expressional purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat animal-figure bases as sculptural inserts judged on their expressive success, not as substitutes for sound architectural base design. Their acceptability depends on successful, context-appropriate execution rather than on architectural rules alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use horizontal bands of color as natural wall-decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: It is perfectly natural that the different kinds of stone used in its successive courses should be of different colors ... They are ... a kind of expression of the growth or age of the wall ... a symbol of the alternation of light and darkness ... valuable as an expression of horizontal space ... and the merely ocular charm of interlineal opposition of color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ alternate horizontal bands of color where constructional differences in stone occur; they provide symbolic and pictorial advantages. This is especially effective for deep, bold courses and is historically noble when honestly derived from materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chiselling joints to create linear ornament; prefer color separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Why should the lines which mark the division of the stones be wrong when they are chiselled, and right when they are marked by color? ... the chiselling of the stones is a wilful throwing away of time and labor ... the building is weaker than it was before ... straight lines are ugly things as lines, but admirable as limits of colored spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not create visual horizontal lines merely by chiselling joints or excessive pointing—the practice weakens the structure and often looks unpleasant. Prefer honest color-based banding or material changes to create linear emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose masonry pattern based on unit size (chequer for small masonry)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the masonry is small, it is better to throw its colors into chequered patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt surface patterning to the scale of the masonry: use chequer patterns for small-unit brickwork; use broad horizontal bands when courses are deep and bold. Examples: Ducal Palace (broad bands), town of Moulins (chequered brickwork).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rustication as a means to fake solidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rustication ... resembles nothing so much as worm casts ... you may, by rustication, make your good marble or granite look like wet slime ... Do not think that nature rusticates her foundations. Smooth sheets of rock ... that is her preparation for first stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on rustication to give an appearance of solidity; it often degrades noble materials' character and is a poor imitation of natural rock. Avoid copying forms of refuse or corruption; rustication is often a sign of degraded taste unless used with true material justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wall ornament must express mass and weight; avoid linear supremacy
rubrics_metrics.description: All good wall ornament ... retains the expression of firm and massive substance, and of broad surface, and ... architecture instantly declined when linear design was substituted for massive, and the sense of weight of wall was lost in a wilderness of upright or undulating rods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure wall decoration preserves the impression of mass and solidity. Do not substitute delicate linear motifs that undermine the wall's apparent weight; successful wall ornament ranges from inlaid geometrical work to bas-relief but must not deny the fundamental mass of the wall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spandril treatments and appropriate options
rubrics_metrics.description: The spandril ... may be pierced with a circle, or with a group of circles ... Sometimes the circle is entirely pierced; at other times it is merely suggested by a mosaic or light tracery ... The other modes of spandril filling may be broadly reduced to four heads: 1. Free figure sculpture; 2. Radiated foliage; 3. Trefoils; and 4. Ordinary wall decoration continued into the spandril space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select spandril treatment from these historically successful categories dependent on scale and context: pierced circular tracery (lightening), figure sculpture (narrative/figural emphasis), radiated foliage or trefoils (ornamental centreing), or continuity of wall decoration. Avoid Renaissance practice of colossal reclining figures in spandrils when unsuited to Gothic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tympanum: place for solemn, consecutive figure sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: In Gothic architecture ... [the tympanum] is ... quite arbitrary; and, as it is generally in a conspicuous position, near the eye, and above the entrance, it is almost always charged with a series of rich figure sculptures, solemn in feeling and consecutive in subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the tympanum as a primary, often narrative sculptural field (analogous to Greek pediments). Compose successive, solemn figure groups appropriate to the building's program; use the plate as the primary locus for important figural statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gable apex mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief difficulty in treating a gable lies in the excessive sharpness of its upper point ... the most beautiful victory I have ever seen obtained over this difficulty was by placing a sharp shield ... at the apex of the gable, which exactly reversed the offensive lines, yet without actually breaking them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soften or reverse the harsh internal meeting of gable lines by a compositional device such as a finial, shield, or other apex form that conceals or reverses the offensive lines while preserving the gable's continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaft decoration guided by proportion and scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal beauty of a shaft is its perfect proportion to its work ... if we cut ornaments in intaglio on its surface, we weaken it; if we leave them in relief, we overcharge it ... decorations are admissible on colossal and on diminutive shafts, which are wrong upon those of middle size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let shaft ornamentation be governed by shaft scale: avoid incised intaglio that weakens mid-sized shafts and avoid excessive relief that overcharges them. Colossal shafts can bear large-scale cutting/sculpture; very small shafts may require some chasing or imagery to avoid looking blank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the 'mean' shaft size as most vulnerable to ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the general rule for shaft decoration ... the mean standard would be of some twenty feet in height, by eight or nine in circumference ... this will be the size on which decoration is most difficult and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat shafts of approximately 20 ft height and 8–9 ft circumference as the most problematic for ornament: avoid both intaglio and over-elaborate relief on these; reserve ornament for shafts significantly larger or smaller than this 'mean' size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaft ornament suitability increases away from mean size
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafts become more and more fit subjects for decoration, as they rise farther above, or fall farther beneath [the mean size], until very small and very vast shafts will both be found to look blank unless they receive some chasing or imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As shafts deviate from the mean (either much larger or much smaller), ornament becomes more acceptable and often necessary to avoid perceived blankness. Scale ornament appropriately to size to maintain structural readability.
